_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and most have a near-miss in another section (Marco's app vs Sinéad's course; Marco's rehearsing vs Ahmed's daily cards). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 2.
title: Never too late
subtitle: Four adults describe learning a new language later in life.

sections.A: Marco, 54, engineer, learning Japanese. My daughter moved to Osaka for work four years ago, and when my first grandchild was born there, I decided I didn't want to be the grandfather who only smiles and nods. I began with a phone app, as everyone does, and after six months I could tell you that the apple was red but not ask the way to the station. What really changed things was an online exchange with a retired teacher in Kyoto: I help her with her English, she helps me with my Japanese. She corrects absolutely everything, which I found hard to accept at first. The writing system, which terrifies most beginners, has turned out to be the part I enjoy most; every character is like a small engineering problem. Speaking is another matter. I still rehearse even simple phone calls in advance, and sometimes I put off making them altogether.
sections.B: Sinéad, 38, learning Portuguese. When we moved to Lisbon for my husband's job, I signed up for a grammar course straight away, and I was a good student: I could conjugate any verb you gave me. Then I tried to buy fish at the market and couldn't understand a single word the woman said back to me. Portuguese as it's spoken here swallows half its vowels, and nobody had warned me. So I changed my approach. I go to the same stalls every week and chat, badly, about the weather and the price of sardines, and the stallholders have more or less adopted me. My two children, who go to a local school, were fluent within a year, and I'll admit I found that quite annoying. Now they correct my pronunciation at dinner, which is humbling, but they're usually right.
sections.C: Ahmed, 67, learning Spanish. I retired from teaching chemistry at sixty-five, and within a few months I could feel my mind getting lazy. My doctor said the best thing I could do was take on something genuinely difficult, so I joined a beginners' Spanish class at the community centre. I'm the oldest there by twenty years. My memory isn't what it was, and a word I learn on Monday has often gone by Thursday, so I write everything on cards and go through them every morning with my coffee. It's slow, but it works. What I hadn't expected was how much I'd enjoy being a student again after forty years at the front of a classroom. I'd forgotten what it feels like not to know the answer, and it has made me rather sorry about how impatient I sometimes was with my own pupils.
sections.D: Lena, 29, learning Korean. I never planned to learn Korean. I started watching Korean dramas during a long winter, and at some point I realised I was catching phrases before the subtitles appeared. I began copying the actors out loud, pausing episodes to repeat lines, and my pronunciation got surprisingly good that way. The trouble was that I had no idea how the language actually worked. When I finally took a few lessons, the teacher told me my accent was excellent but that I spoke like a sixty-year-old villain in a soap opera, which was not quite the impression I wanted to give. Now I'm filling in the grammar properly. I've also made friends through an online fan forum, and we talk every week. I've never met any of them, but they've been more patient with me than anyone in a classroom.

questions.question: Which person began learning after being advised to take on a challenge?
questions.why: 'My doctor said the best thing I could do was take on something genuinely difficult.' Marco chose to learn; nobody advised him.

questions.question: Which person discovered that formal study had not prepared them for everyday conversation?
questions.why: A good grammar student who 'couldn't understand a single word' at the market. Marco's app is not formal study, and he learned to read it, not to listen.

questions.question: Which person learned how the language sounds before learning how it works?
questions.why: Her pronunciation 'got surprisingly good' from copying actors, but she 'had no idea how the language actually worked'.

questions.question: Which person most enjoys the part of the language that worries many learners?
questions.why: 'The writing system, which terrifies most beginners, has turned out to be the part I enjoy most.'

questions.question: Which person relies on a daily habit to make up for a weakness?
questions.why: Words disappear by Thursday, so he goes through his cards 'every morning with my coffee'. Marco's rehearsing is not daily, and he often avoids the calls.

questions.question: Which person admits to sometimes avoiding a situation they find difficult?
questions.why: 'sometimes I put off making them altogether': the phone calls. Ahmed's difficulty is memory, and he deals with it every morning.

questions.question: Which person was at first irritated by how quickly family members learned?
questions.why: Her children 'were fluent within a year, and I'll admit I found that quite annoying'.

questions.question: Which person was told that their way of speaking gave the wrong impression?
questions.why: She 'spoke like a sixty-year-old villain in a soap opera, which was not quite the impression I wanted to give'. Sinéad's children correct sounds, not the impression she gives.

questions.question: Which person says the experience has made them think differently about their past behaviour?
questions.why: Being a student again 'has made me rather sorry about how impatient I sometimes was with my own pupils'.

questions.question: Which person has had more support from people they have never met than from teachers?
questions.why: Her online friends, whom she has 'never met', 'they've been more patient with me than anyone in a classroom'. Marco's exchange partner is a teacher who corrects everything.
